 SAFF semis fail to sell out, gate sales raise breach fears
 Published : 14 November 2026
 • 
 Updated : 14 November 2026, 14:44
 • 
 FOOTBALL
 SHARE 
 Sports Reporter 
 Photo: STAR 
 Ticketing arrangements and crowd management at the National Stadium have come under fresh scrutiny ahead of Saturday's SAFF Championship semifinals, with a significant number of seats still available despite organisers promoting sales at the stadium gates. 
 The concerns follow Wednesday's chaotic Bangladesh-Sri Lanka encounter, when frustrated supporters breached security barricades and forced their way into the galleries, even as several sections of the lower stands remained visibly empty. 
 Tap here to add The Daily Star as a trusted source 
 With Bangladesh set to face Pakistan tonight, the prospect of another large crowd has raised questions over whether organisers have taken adequate steps to prevent a repeat.
 Tickify, the tournament's ticketing partner, took to Facebook around 12:30pm today to announce that tickets would be available at the stadium gates alongside online sales, just like the previous matchday. The announcement came barely an hour before the gates were scheduled to open at 1:30pm. 
 Yet, around midday, its website continued to show substantial availability across several sections of the venue.
 Image 
 Four of the six general gallery sections were marked as sold out, but 11 blocks remained available across the South West Lower and East Gallery Lower sections. Tickets were also available in the more expensive Club House and VIP categories, with several blocks in those sections yet to be sold.
 The apparent disconnect between the online inventory and the promotion of physical sales raises an obvious question: are tickets being reserved for walk-in buyers, or has demand simply failed to meet expectations? 
 The pricing structure presents another hurdle. After complaints over ticket prices and visibly sparse stands during the group stage, the minimum gallery price was reduced from Tk 1,000 to Tk 800 for gate sales on Wednesday. For the semifinals, however, the base gallery price remains Tk 999. With Tickify's Tk 64 service fee, the cheapest ticket costs Tk 1,063. Club House and VIP tickets come to Tk 4,063 and Tk 7,063 respectively, including the fee.
 TSA Sports & Entertainment, which holds the tournament's marketing rights, had reported around 11,000 tickets sold by Thursday. With the competition now at the semifinal stage, the continued availability of seats raises questions about whether the organisers have got their pricing and sales strategy right.
 The presence of Hamza Choudhury, Shamit Shome and Farhan Ali has added to the anticipation around the national team, but that enthusiasm has yet to translate into a sell-out.
 More alarming is the prospect of another security breakdown. Wednesday's India-Maldives afternoon fixture drew a sparse crowd, but thousands of supporters began gathering around the stadium ahead of Bangladesh's evening match. Frustrated by the arrangements, sections of the crowd overwhelmed security personnel and breached barricades at Gates 3 and 4. Chants of 'Bhuya' rang out amid the chaos as supporters forced their way into the galleries. Gate 4 was eventually locked, leaving some ticket-holding spectators outside until the crowd surged through.
 Image 
 Yet, despite the breach and the rush into the stands, several sections of the lower galleries remained visibly empty during the Bangladesh-Sri Lanka match. The contrast was difficult to miss: supporters struggling to get inside, security personnel losing control at the gates, and vacant seats inside the stadium. 
 It raised serious questions about ticket distribution, entry arrangements and the organisers' ability to make effective use of the available seating.
 Today's double-header presents another major test. India face Bhutan in the first semifinal, officially scheduled for 3:30pm, while Bangladesh take on Pakistan at 8:30pm. 
 The National Stadium is expected to draw another sizeable crowd for Bangladesh's semifinal. The organisers now have a responsibility to ensure that supporters can enter safely, ticket-holders are not left stranded outside and the disorder witnessed on Wednesday is not repeated. Another failure would be difficult to explain away as a one-off lapse.
